fact_text: The government plans to auction 527.2 MHz of spectrum, sold as bandwidth across six bands, with the auction stated in the video as taking place on 10 March 2026.
source_name: Nukta Business, 'Pakistan's Internet Spectrum Auction Explained in Under 10 Minutes | Nukta Business' (YouTube, 2026-03-09)

fact_text: The six spectrum bands in the auction are 700, 1800, 2100, 2300, 2600 and 3500 MHz, and each band is a set of frequencies that is exclusively allocated to a telecom operator.
source_name: Nukta Business, 'Pakistan's Internet Spectrum Auction Explained in Under 10 Minutes | Nukta Business' (YouTube, 2026-03-09)

fact_text: Higher-frequency radio waves carry more data but cover shorter distances, so urban cell networks prefer them, while lower-frequency waves suit rural areas with widely spaced towers.
source_name: Nukta Business, 'Pakistan's Internet Spectrum Auction Explained in Under 10 Minutes | Nukta Business' (YouTube, 2026-03-09)

fact_text: In the 2100 MHz band, which runs from 1920 to 2170 MHz, Jazz, Telenor, Zong and UFone hold allocated blocks, and the yellow blocks shown in the video are unallocated.
source_name: Nukta Business, 'Pakistan's Internet Spectrum Auction Explained in Under 10 Minutes | Nukta Business' (YouTube, 2026-03-09)

fact_text: The unallocated 2100 MHz blocks are seen as idle capacity, and allocating them would give operators more data capacity, although the speed effect will only be clear later.
source_name: Nukta Business, 'Pakistan's Internet Spectrum Auction Explained in Under 10 Minutes | Nukta Business' (YouTube, 2026-03-09)

fact_text: Mobile data travels from the phone as radio waves to the nearest cell tower, then by fibre optic cable to a data centre, which can be abroad and linked by submarine cable.
source_name: Nukta Business, 'Pakistan's Internet Spectrum Auction Explained in Under 10 Minutes | Nukta Business' (YouTube, 2026-03-09)
